topic: Move Operations Not Present Failure: User-Defined Copy/Dtor
explanation: A critical anti-pattern is the assumption that move operations (constructor and assignment) are automatically generated by the compiler if the class does not define them. The reality is that the presence of user-declared special member functions can suppress the generation of move operations. Specifically, if a class declares any of the following—a copy constructor, copy assignment operator, or destructor—the compiler will often *not* generate the move constructor and move assignment operator (pre-C++11, and conditional in C++11/14/17 rules). This failure state is common in legacy code or when developers update older classes by adding only a destructor (e.g., for logging or resource cleanup) without explicitly defining or defaulting the move operations. When move operations are suppressed, any attempt to use `std::move` or rely on move semantics for that class will silently fall back to calling the copy operations (if they exist). This failure completely nullifies the performance benefits of move semantics, forcing expensive resource duplication instead of transfer. The underlying failure is the developer's misplaced reliance on compiler defaults without verifying the five special member functions (The Rule of Five/Zero).
practical_example: A large-scale refactoring project relies on modern compiler optimization, but fails to gain expected performance. Profiling reveals that 80% of data transfers are deep copies because the underlying utility classes, which had inherited from older C++ standards, defined custom destructors for trivial cleanup, implicitly disabling the move constructors across the entire system.
chapter: Item 29: Assume that move operations are not present, not cheap, and not used
